title: Ada and the Smile
premise: Elodie Galloway, a pest controller with twenty years of rational explanations in his toolkit, is hired to investigate sounds in the cellar of a house where something leaves fingerprints at child height. When his overnight audio equipment records a second voice answering questions no one asked aloud, he learns the entity is Ada, a girl who vanished in 1974, and that the homeowner's family took something from her before she fell down the old well. As Elodie digs into the town's buried complicity, his duty to stay invisible collides with his growing loyalty to a dead child's truth. In the end, Elodie returns Ada's stolen locket to the well on the night it refills, trading his own silence for her release—and the voice that answers his final recording is his own.
about_author: Bram Marchetti is the pen name of a former building inspector who spent a decade documenting condemned houses across the Rust Belt. Their fiction draws on the things found behind walls that never made it into official reports.

chapters.title: Fingerprints at Child Height
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. Called to the Harrow house for 'rodents,' Elodie finds greasy handprints on the cellar wall—small, human, too high for a child to reach without help. He files it as raccoon damage and takes the job anyway, needing the money. Emotional beat: professional denial cracking at its first seam.

chapters.title: The Recording Nobody Asked For
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. Leaving overnight audio gear per contract, Elodie reviews the footage: scratching, then a small voice asking, 'Is she coming back?'—and a second voice, wet and low, answering. He tells himself it's interference. Emotional beat: dread disguised as troubleshooting; the first question he can't explain away.

chapters.title: What the Well Kept
chapters.summary: POV alternating Elodie and county archive fragments. Researching the property, Elodie learns a girl named Ada Voss disappeared in 1974; the well was capped the same autumn by the Harrows' father. The fingerprints match missing-person photos. Emotional beat: grief arriving twenty years late, through someone else's file.

chapters.title: Duty of Care
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. Mrs. Harrow begs him to keep working quietly—her son sleeps in the cellar now, talking in his sleep. Elodie's license, his reputation, his careful invisibility all argue for walking away. He signs a second month instead. Emotional beat: love against duty, choosing the boy over his own safety.

chapters.title: Questions in the Dark
chapters.summary: POV Elodie, intercut with transcript pages. Elodie begins leaving questions on the recorder: What was taken? Who took it? The answers come at 3:11 a.m., always three words or fewer. The voice knows his name. Emotional beat: intimacy with the impossible; loyalty forming toward a dead girl.

chapters.title: The Locket
chapters.summary: POV Elodie and Mrs. Harrow. Confronted, Mrs. Harrow admits her father stole Ada's silver locket the day she vanished—buried it under the cellar floor to 'keep her quiet.' She gives him a spade and a warning: the well refills every October. Emotional beat: justice outside the law demanded from inside a family's guilt.

chapters.title: Twenty Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: POV Elodie, flashback-heavy. Elodie excavates the floorboards while remembering every noise he ever explained away—including one in his own childhood home. The locket surfaces, warm. Behind him, the stairs creak under nothing. Emotional beat: the collapse of a life built on plausible deniability.

chapters.title: Refill
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. October arrives early; rain floods the town, and the well cap weeps water upward. The second voice grows louder in every room, no longer content with recordings. The boy goes missing from his bed. Emotional beat: rising panic as the deadline stops being metaphorical.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. Climax. Elodie carries the locket and the boy down into the flooding cellar, past the thing wearing Ada's shape and something older wearing its patience. It demands not the locket but a confession spoken aloud—the town's, his own. He gives both, naming what he explained away at nine years old. Emotional beat: truth as the only currency the dark accepts.

chapters.title: The Last Recording
chapters.summary: POV Elodie, epistolary epilogue. The boy wakes safe; the prints fade; the well runs dry and stays dry. Elodie plays his final tape: silence, then his own voice answering a question he doesn't remember asking. He mails the transcripts to Ada's surviving sister and keeps listening. Emotional beat: quiet, haunted peace—loyalty outlasting the haunting.
